name: Sternocleidomastoid (SCM) hypertrophy

lead: The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) is the prominent muscle running from behind the ear down to the collarbone and breastbone on each side of the neck. Looksmaxxers build it to get a thicker, more defined neck.

The SCM rotates and tilts the head and flexes the neck, so training for it is generally discussed as resistance work for those movements. Anatomy sources describe the muscle's attachments, nerve supply and function; no study has examined deliberate SCM hypertrophy.

paras: People train neck rotation, tilt and flexion with resistance such as hands, bands or weights as part of a physique routine, combined with the diet and training that drive muscle gain elsewhere. Visible change in neck size generally takes months.
No cosmetic-specific risks are documented. Neck loading is generally regarded by clinicians as requiring care in people with cervical spine problems.

angle.text: Training the sternocleidomastoid, the large muscle on each side of the neck, grows it so the sides of the neck look thicker and more defined. The muscle's anatomy and function are well described.

lead: The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) is one of the largest and most superficial muscles of the neck, running on each side from the sternum and clavicle up to the mastoid process behind the ear.[1] In looksmaxxing culture, SCM hypertrophy means building these muscles so the sides of the neck look thicker and more defined, which proponents say gives a more imposing, masculine look and adds width beneath the jaw and head.

Anatomy references describe the SCM as the most striking landmark on the side of the neck, and report that average neck circumference differs between men and women, attributed to muscle mass, BMI and higher testosterone in men.[2] People who train necks typically do it through flexion, extension and lateral work, and sometimes bridges, alongside overall strength training, as seen in lifting forums.[3][4]
No published study located has examined deliberate SCM hypertrophy or its effect on appearance.
infobox: Mastoid process and superior nuchal line
Head rotation and tilt; neck flexion (both sides); accessory breathing

paras: The muscle has two heads, a sternal head from the upper front of the manubrium and a clavicular head from the medial third of the clavicle, which merge into one rounded belly and insert on the mastoid process and the occipital bone.[1] The clavicular head varies in width between individuals.[1] It is clearly visible when the head rotates and forms a landmark that divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.[1][2]

Acting on one side it turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it toward the same side; acting together the two muscles flex the neck, and they help in forced inhalation as accessory breathing muscles.[1]

Wikipedia gives average neck circumference of about 38.7 cm in men and 33.3 cm in women, attributing the gap mainly to body composition, muscle mass and BMI, plus higher testosterone, which promotes neck muscle growth.[2] The article describes the sternomastoid as the most striking mark on the side of the neck.[2] It does not discuss neck training for cosmetic purposes.[2]

A 2005 T Nation thread has a lifter asking for neck-training suggestions, saying he does flexion, extension and lateral movements with a plate against his head and wants to develop the SCM because he feels it will give his traps a higher look and help injury protection.[3]

In a later T Nation thread on targeting the sternocleidomastoid, the original poster reports his neck growing from 15.5 to 16.5 inches in a month using side curls, flexion and extension, and sets a goal of a 19-inch neck. Replies differ: one poster says a thin neck might need about 40 lbs more lean mass to reach that size, another recommends building the squat and deadlift first and calls neck harnesses dangerous, one says not to bother targeting the SCM, and another argues direct SCM training is a bad idea in people with forward head posture, preferring posture work and deep neck flexor strength.[4] Another poster in the thread says his neck reached 19.5 inches without direct neck work.[4]
No studies found. Clinical literature on the SCM concerns conditions such as torticollis and its role in neurological examination, not cosmetic hypertrophy.[1]

lore.intro: Neck and SCM training is discussed in strength forums as a way to build a bigger-looking frame, with opinions divided on whether the SCM should be targeted directly.[3][4]
